As universities continue to evolve and adapt to the ever-changing landscape of higher education, one question that has been increasingly discussed is whether academic English courses should be eliminated. While these courses have traditionally been seen as a necessary stepping stone for non-native English speakers to succeed in the academic world, in the modern world, they may no longer be necessary.

First and foremost, the proliferation of technology has made it easier than ever for students to learn and improve their English language skills outside of a formal academic setting. With the availability of online resources such as language learning apps, tutoring services, and virtual language exchange programs, students can now access high-quality language instruction from the comfort of their own homes. This means that even if a student is not proficient in English when they begin their university studies, they can quickly catch up and become proficient through self-study and independent learning.

Furthermore, many universities now offer English language support services such as writing centers and language labs, which can provide students with the additional support they need to succeed in their coursework. These services are often staffed by trained professionals who can help students improve their language skills and overcome any challenges they may be facing in their classes.

Another argument against academic English courses is that they can create a barrier for non-native English speakers who may feel intimidated or self-conscious about taking a class specifically for English language learners. This can lead to feelings of isolation and disconnection from their peers, which can be detrimental to their academic and social success. By eliminating academic English courses, universities can create a more inclusive and welcoming environment for all students, regardless of their language proficiency.

In conclusion, academic English courses  should be closed.
